newsitem.title: USA: US High Court to hear appeal by ex-asbestos makers.
newsitem.headline: US High Court to hear appeal by ex-asbestos makers.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear an appeal by 20 former asbestos manufacturers of a ruling that threw out a proposed $1.3 billion settlement involving an estimated 100,000 personal injury claims.

The justices said they would review a ruling last May by a U.S. appeals court in Philadelphia that the settlement raises questions of fairness about how it treats people with future claims who have been exposed to asbestos, but are not yet sick.
The companies asked the Supreme Court to hear the case and overturn the appeals court's decision, The justices will hear arguments early next year, with a decision due by July.

The proposed settlement had been reached in 1993 by lawyers for a group of people who had been exposed to asbestos and 20 firms that stopped making asbestos products around 1975, including Armstrong World Industries Inc, Union Carbide Corp, Dana Corp and Pfizer Inc.

The settlement would have provided a range of payments for those who made claims after the case was filed and who met certain criteria for medical ailments and exposure to asbestos, which has been linked to cancer and other illnesses.

The proposed settlement set caps on the amount of money an individual victim may recover and on how many claims may be paid out in a year. An estimated 100,000 people would have received payments over a 10-year period.
The settlement did not provide any payments for those who had been exposed to asbestos, but are not yet sick. It did remove the statute of limitations on when they could file claims.

A federal judge approved the settlement in 1994, but the appeals court said it was wrong to include in the settlement those already suffering asbestos-related diseases with people who are not yet sick. It also held that the problem of asbestos litigation cannot be solved in the courts, but should be addressed by Congress.
Attorneys for the companies said in their appeal to the Supreme Court that the appeals court decision "throws the law governing class action settlements into complete confusion."
They said the appeals court decision will result in the filing of "tens of thousands" of claims against the firms in federal and state courts.
"The courts, litigants and public will again be condemned to an asbestos litigation quagmire," their appeal said.
Three business groups -- the Chamber of Commerce, the Chemical Manufacturers Association and the National Association of Manufacturers -- supported the appeal.

Harvard University law professor Laurence Tribe and the Public Citizen Litigation Group, both representing various individuals or groups opposed to the settlement, urged the justices to turn down the appeal.
They said the settlement "would extinguish" future claims by those who develop asbestos-linked diseases.
